correctness.rationale: For a generic central normal u, every section vertex is exactly one polytope edge whose endpoint signs are opposite. Crossing the great circle u·v=0 for vertex v and its antipode -v changes this count by -2 times the neighbor-sign imbalance at v. If the count is constant, this sign sum must vanish for all generic u in v^perp. The planar sign-jump lemma implies that the nonzero projected neighbor directions at v occur in antipodal pairs, with multiplicity. Each original edge spans a unique origin plane H, and local pairing gives degree exactly two for the polytope-edge subgraph inside H; convexity of the polygon P∩H means any such edge cycle must cover its entire polygon boundary, yielding disjoint equatorial belts partitioning every edge. Conversely a generic central plane crosses the boundary of each centered belt polygon at exactly two genuine polytope edges, so N_P(u)=2r for r belts. This establishes all three equivalences for every full-dimensional centrally symmetric convex 3-polytope, not merely tested examples. The assigned exact-arithmetic Python source was inspected: its Q(sqrt5) polyhedron construction checks the regular octahedron (3 square belts), cuboctahedron (4 hexagonal belts) and icosidodecahedron (6 decagonal belts) with generic normal tests. The cube witness has 4 and 6 section edges and distinguishes central sections from orthogonal shadows. Finite examples are not used as proof of the general implication.
residual_risks: No assertion for nongeneric central sections through vertices, noncentrally symmetric polytopes or higher dimensions.
The equatorial belting criterion is combinatorial; it does not guarantee equal section areas or metric shapes.
